issue_title: Support custom per-class decision thresholds and a rejection option in `sklearn.metrics.confusion_matrix` and `sklearn.metrics.ConfusionMatrixDisplay`.
issue_body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Currently, in the code, the confusion matrix implementation relies on discrete predictions of y_pred on the basis of either 'argmax' for multi-class or a scalar cutoff value. 
In many real-world, risk-sensitive machine learning workflows (e.g., fraud detection, medical diagnostics, or financial compliance), models operate under a selective classification paradigm ("classification with a rejection option"). 



### Describe your proposed solution

With this issue, I propose a custom parameter 'thresholds' to 'confusion_matrix' and it's visual counterparts that are ConfusionMatrixDisplay 'from_estimator', and 'from_predictions' that accepts a custom decision boundary for per class label prediction , along side the 'y_score'.

Parameter:
thresholds can be an array-like of shape (n_classes,) or a dict, with a default of None. It accepts an array of threshold floats corresponding to target classes or a dictionary mapping class labels to float thresholds. When thresholds is provided, the function accepts 2D probability or score arrays (y_score) of shape (n_samples, n_classes).

Rejection region:
For any sample that is rejected out of any class label, expand the matrix by n+1 , or append a rejection column for predictions. Display labels dynamically update to include 'Unassigned' for string or categorical targets, or -1 for integer targets.

 

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

None

### Additional context

_No response_

judgment.summary: The issue proposes adding support for custom per-class decision thresholds and a rejection option (selective classification) in `confusion_matrix` and `ConfusionMatrixDisplay`.
judgment.rationale: This is a detailed feature request proposing API enhancements to the metrics module, specifically `confusion_matrix` and its display utility, to support custom thresholds and rejection regions. The label 'module:metrics' is the most specific fit.

issue_title: adding weights to the calculation for Ledoit Wolf
issue_body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Ledoit Wolf is a method for shrinking the empirical covariace matrix for data, and is already available in this library. The process essentially does three steps:
1) make the empirical covariance matrix
2) calculates some parameters (beta / delta) that are then used to calculate the shrinkage coefficient
3) use the results from steps (1) and (2) to make the desired output.

Given random p-vector X,  step (1) is just doing E[ X X^T ) - E[ X ] E[X^T ] the way you expect. Step (2) is calculating variables beta and delta that invariably involve calculating E[ X_i X_j ] and E[ X^2_i X^2_j ], just with a typical mean calculation. What I am proposing is extending these calculations, where weights can be leveraged to do the expected value calculations. This will allow the user to, for example, do the calculation on the exponentially weighted covariance matrix, but really use any weighting they choose. By setting weights = np.ones( X.shape[0] ) by default, we can maintain the current standard output. If desired, this procedure might possibly be extended to OAS (another shrinkage matrix).

### Describe your proposed solution

I am proposing adding the named variable "weights" to the "fit" function inputs for the LedoitWolf class (and any other necessary changes under the hood).

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

judgment.summary: Request to add support for sample weights in the LedoitWolf covariance estimator to allow calculations like exponentially weighted covariance.
judgment.rationale: The issue proposes adding a 'weights' parameter to the 'fit' method of the LedoitWolf estimator to support weighted covariance calculations. This falls under the covariance module.

issue_title: Document tie-breaking behavior for max_categories in OneHotEncoder/OrdinalEncoder infrequent category grouping
issue_body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation



When `max_categories` forces additional categories into the infrequent group beyond what `min_frequency` alone would select, and multiple categories are tied in count at the cutoff boundary, the docs for `max_categories` don't specify which tied category is kept as frequent vs. grouped as infrequent.

Looking at `_identify_infrequent()` in `sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py`, the tie-break is implicit rather than documented:

```python
# stable sort to preserve original count order
smallest_levels = np.argsort(category_count, kind="mergesort")[:-frequent_category_count]
infrequent_mask[smallest_levels] = True
```

Counts are sorted using `np.argsort(category_count, kind="mergesort")` — a stable sort — so ties are resolved by the order categories appear in `categories_[i]`, which for `categories='auto'` is lexicographic/numeric sort order. This behavior is not mentioned in the `max_categories` docstring or the User Guide section on infrequent categories (`encoder_infrequent_categories`).

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Add a sentence to the `max_categories` parameter docs (in both `OneHotEncoder` and `OrdinalEncoder`) and to the User Guide section on infrequent categories, stating that ties in category count are broken using the sort order of the categories (via a stable sort). This is also relevant to the discussion in #32161.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

X = np.array([["a"] * 2 + ["b"] * 2 + ["c"] * 5], dtype=object).T
enc = OneHotEncoder(max_categories=2, sparse_output=False).fit(X)
print(enc.infrequent_categories_)
# 'a' and 'b' tie at count=2 -- which one is grouped as infrequent
# is not documented, though it is deterministic.
```

### Additional context

Related: #32161 discusses tie-breaking by lexicographical order for encoder category ordering more broadly.

judgment.summary: Request to document the tie-breaking behavior for `max_categories` in `OneHotEncoder` and `OrdinalEncoder` when multiple categories have the same count at the cutoff boundary.
judgment.rationale: This is a request to clarify and document existing, deterministic behavior (tie-breaking via stable sort) in the documentation and User Guide for encoders. Since it is a documentation improvement and does not report a bug or crash, it is classified as low priority.

issue_title: RFC: Unknown categories should not inherit the meaning of missing values in HGB / trees
issue_body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

`HistGradientBoosting*` and `DecisionTree*` (native categorical support) both encode a categorical column such that **a category never seen during `fit` is mapped to the exact same internal value as an actual missing value**, inheriting whatever *meaning* missing values happened to have during training. Let's call this policy A.

This is fine when missingness carries no signal. When it does (a common real-world pattern), it's actively harmful: a brand new, unrelated category at prediction time gets confidently assigned the *missing*-value prediction instead of an uncertain/neutral one.

I experimented with an alternative policy (B): consider missing values as a category of its own (so just a normal category) and encode it as an integer, and encode unknown values as NaNs.

I could not find a real case example where B underperforms A, but I did find an example where B outperforms A
(KDD cup 2009 dataset, churn target, select one single column with informative missing values as X)

I propose to adopt policy B. It's a small behavior change but I don't think it can break or hurt any existing user code.
Note that we made [a bigger and ill-documented one](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34663) on HGB native categorical support and nobody complained... (and this one could have terribly hurt some ML pipelines).

I think the current impact is low because the likelihood of having unknown categories is low for categorical features of at most 255 distinct categories (which is the current limitation for native categorical support). But with #33972, this 255 limitation is removed for extra-trees (which is great) and the impact of policy A vs B becomes more important.

Note: implementing policy B cleanly with an `OrdinalEncoder` is currently not possible, which is one of the thing that makes me think that we should move forwards on those two issues:
- https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/28892
- https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34387

judgment.summary: This issue proposes changing how tree-based models with native categorical support handle unknown categories, suggesting they should not inherit the same internal representation as missing values.
judgment.rationale: The issue is explicitly framed as an RFC (Request for Comments) proposing a design change to the categorical encoding behavior in HistGradientBoosting and Decision Trees. 'RFC' is the most appropriate label, and the priority is medium as it involves a significant design discussion.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Using a `ScoringMonitor` in a lot of sub-estimators in sub-processes eventually raises an `EOFError` when trying to create the connection for the callback to communicate across processes.

After investigating with the help of an LLM, the suspect appears to be the `_worker_connections`. It stores new connections for each fit, but there is no mechanism to remove them from the cache. When persistent workers are used, like when using joblib's loky backend, the cache grows until the worker process hits its fd limit and the next time a connection is opened the handshake sequence breaks mid-flight, causing the EOFError.

The LLM's suggested fix is to have a max size for `_worker_connections`, using a least recently used eviction policy.

issue_title: PRF: Over-subscription in pairwise_distances with `backend="threading"` + BLAS-pthreads
issue_body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

`sklearn.metrics.pairwise_distances` accepts a `n_jobs` parameters and uses `joblib.Parallel(backend="threading", n_jobs=n_jobs)` under-the-hood. But this parallelization happens on top on openBLAS parallelism, and can lead to what looks like over-subscription.

(but maybe it's not over-subscription, and something else, like cost of repeated small parallelized blas calls, etc. I haven't investigated) 

Results from a small benchmark script shows that limiting blas to 1 thread helps scaling as `n_jobs` grows (and usually achieves best performance compared to n_jobs=1 with blas parallelism enabled):

``` 
--- n_samples=2000  n_features=200 ---
  n_jobs=  1 | pin-blas=0:      33ms
```

> There should be no logic, not even input validation, and the parameters should not be changed; which also means ideally they should not be mutable objects such as lists or dictionaries. If they’re mutable, they should be copied before being modified. The corresponding logic should be put where the parameters are used, typically in `fit`.

Certain edits to these rules pass the `check_estimator` associated tests but fail elsewhere, e.g., subtle changes to the object type. Below, I show examples where this violation from API compliance is caught indirectly in `fit` on edge cases but not under the test suite for API compliance.

issue_title: [FEA] Add Ambiguity Range metric for safety-critical classification
issue_body: > [!WARNING] > This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label. ### Describe the workflow you want to enable Practitioners in safety-critical fields—such as medical diagnostics, structural engineering, or high-stakes financial modeling—require a method to explicitly quantify the "Indecision Zone" of a binary classifier. While aggregate metrics like the F1-score or Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) provide a high-level view of model performance, they often mask the specific regions where a model's prediction is statistically equivalent to guessing. By implementing the ambiguity_range_score, we enable a Tri-Modal Decision Workflow: Automated Action (High Confidence): Samples with scores above the Upper Threshold ($T_{upper}$, representing 100% Precision) or below the Lower Threshold ($T_{lower}$, representing 100% Recall) are handled automatically by the system with high trust. Human-in-the-Loop (Ambiguity Zone): Samples falling within the range $\mathcal{A} = T_{upper} - T_{lower}$ are flagged for manual expert review. Reliability Benchmarking: This allows developers to select models that minimize required human intervention by reducing the Ambiguity Range, even in cases where traditional metrics like AUC remain static. Safety-Critical Calibration: Practitioners can visualize exactly how much of a population falls into a "Gray Zone" where the model cannot guarantee a certain outcome. ### Describe your proposed solution I propose adding a new metric: ambiguity_range_score(y_true, y_score, *, epsilon=0.0, pos_label=None). Key Technical Implementations: The Ambiguity Measure ($\mathcal{A}$): Defined as the difference between the threshold required for perfect precision and the threshold required for perfect recall. Epsilon ($\epsilon$) Robustness: To handle real-world datasets containing outliers or label noise, the epsilon parameter allows for a "Soft Ambiguity" measure (e.g., $\epsilon=0.01$ for 99% precision/recall). This prevents a single mislabeled data point from artificially maximizing the range to 1.0. Integration: The function utilizes the existing precision_recall_curve logic to find the critical boundary points, ensuring consistency with scikit-learn’s internal API. ### Threshold Independence & Model Robustness A common limitation of standard classification metrics is their dependence on an arbitrary decision threshold (e.g., 0.5). Choosing a single threshold is often a heuristic choice made during deployment that may not reflect the inherent separability of the model. The ambiguity_range_score is superior in this regard because it is threshold-independent. Rather than evaluating performance at a single point, it quantifies the "Indecision Zone" as a global characteristic of the model's feature-space quality. By measuring the distance between the two extreme bounds of reliability ($T_{upper}$ and $T_{lower}$), it provides a scalar value that describes model "resoluteness" regardless of where an individual user might eventually set their operating point. ### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant I have considered using the Detection Error Tradeoff (DET) curve; however, while DET curves are excellent for visual analysis, they do not provide a direct, scalar "range" value that can be easily used for automated model selection or as a clear KPI for "Human-in-the-Loop" resource planning. ### Additional context I have attached a figure that provides an empirical verification of the metric: Distribution Density Plot: Illustrates the score overlapping that generates the Ambiguity Range ($\mathcal{A}$) and the resulting Ternary Decision Logic. Sensitivity Analysis: Demonstrates how the metric responds to increasing Label Noise vs. Feature Noise, and confirms that the epsilon parameter successfully maintains metric robustness in noisy environments. Developed and proposed by Kian Maleki. Here is the proposed implementation for `ambiguity_range_score`: ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.utils import check_consistent_length from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve def ambiguity_range_score(y_true, y_score, *, epsilon=0.0, pos_label=None): """Compute the Ambiguity Measure between perfect precision and recall. The Ambiguity Measure is the difference between the threshold required for perfect precision and the threshold required for perfect recall. Parameters ---------- y_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,) True binary labels. y_score : array-like of shape (n_samples,) Target scores, can either be probability estimates of the positive class or confidence values. epsilon : float, default=0.0 The tolerance for "perfect" metrics. (e.g., 0.01 for 99% precision/recall). pos_label : int, float, bool or str, default=None The label of the positive class. Returns ------- ambiguity : float The calculated range between thresholds. A smaller value indicates better class separability. """ check_consistent_length(y_true, y_score) # Calculate Precision-Recall curve and thresholds precision, recall, thresholds = precision_recall_curve( y_true, y_score, pos_label=pos_label ) # 1. Upper Threshold: Minimum score where Precision >= 1 - epsilon target_p = 1.0 - epsilon p_indices = np.where(precision >= target_p)[0] # Clip index for thresholds t_upper = thresholds[p_indices[0]] if p_indices.size > 0 else np.max(y_score) # 2. Lower Threshold: Maximum score where Recall >= 1 - epsilon target_r = 1.0 - epsilon r_indices = np.where(recall >= target_r)[0] t_lower = thresholds[r_indices[-1]] if r_indices.size > 0 else np.min(y_score) # 3. Ambiguity Measure return float(t_upper - t_lower) # Example Usage: if __name__ == "__main__": y_true = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1]) y_scores = np.array([0.1, 0.4, 0.35, 0.8]) print(f"Ambiguity Measure: {ambiguity_range_score(y_true, y_scores)}")

judgment.summary: A feature request proposing the addition of `ambiguity_range_score`, a new metric to quantify the 'Indecision Zone' (the threshold range between perfect precision and perfect recall) for binary classifiers.
judgment.rationale: The issue proposes a new metric for evaluating binary classifiers, which directly relates to the `module:metrics` module. As a new feature request for a specialized metric, it is classified as low priority.

issue_title: Birch: subcluster radius is numerically unstable far from the origin — clustering is not translation-invariant
issue_body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

**``Birch``**  derives each subcluster's squared radius from the **non-centered** second moment, `r² = Σᵢ‖xᵢ‖²/n − ‖c‖²` (`_CFSubcluster.merge_subcluster` in `sklearn/cluster/_birch.py`). Both terms scale like ‖offset‖², so far from the origin they are large and nearly equal, and their float64 difference loses the unit-scale variance to **catastrophic cancellation**. `r²` then reads noise (often negative → clamped to 0), so `threshold` no longer bounds the leaf radius and the CF-tree silently changes structure. Concretely, a **pure translation** of the input — which cannot change Birch's result in exact arithmetic — changes the number of subclusters.



### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np, sklearn
from sklearn.cluster import Birch

rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X = np.vstack([rng.randn(200, 2), rng.randn(200, 2) + [15.0, 0.0]])  # two tight blobs, spread ~1

base = len(Birch(threshold=1.0, n_clusters=None).fit(X).subcluster_centers_)
print(f"sklearn {sklearn.__version__}  baseline (offset 0): {base} subclusters")
for off in (1e5, 1e6, 1e7, 1e8):
    n = len(Birch(threshold=1.0, n_clusters=None).fit(X + off).subcluster_centers_)
    print(f"  offset={off:.0e}: {n:4d}  {'OK' if n == base else 'DEGRADED'}")
```

### Expected Results

The subcluster count is invariant under translation (Birch's `threshold` test is translation-equivariant in exact arithmetic): `12` at every offset.

### Actual Results

```
sklearn 1.9.0  baseline (offset 0): 12 subclusters
  offset=1e+05:   12  OK
  offset=1e+06:   13  DEGRADED
  offset=1e+07:   11  DEGRADED
  offset=1e+08:   99  DEGRADED
```


### Versions

```shell
   machine: Linux-7.0.14-201.fc44.x86_64-x86_64-with-glibc2.43

threading_layer: pthreads

       user_api: openmp
   internal_api: openmp
    num_threads: 16
         prefix: libgomp
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I'd be glad to work on the PR. The cancellation is in `new_ss / new_n − new_sq_norm`, from accumulating `squared_sum_` as raw `Σ‖x‖²`. The standard remedy: store the **centered** second moment `Σᵢ‖xᵢ − c‖²` and combine subclusters with the numerically stable **parallel-axis (Chan et al.) update** — the common offset cancels *before* squaring. With that (a Python-only change to `_birch.py`) the MRE stays exactly invariant through offset **1e7** (vs 1e6 today), a ~100× extension; `1e8` still degrades but less (66 vs 99) — the residual is the fundamental float64 limit (unit spread ≈ 10 ULP at 1e8), not the formula. This is the instability and fix documented in **BETULA** (Lang & Schubert, *"BETULA: Numerically Stable CF-Trees for BIRCH Clustering"*, SISAP 2020 / Information Systems 2021). Ready implementation in #34433 (closed pending this issue, per @virchan) — happy to re-submit once scope is agreed

judgment.summary: The Birch clustering algorithm suffers from numerical instability and catastrophic cancellation when calculating subcluster radii far from the origin, making the clustering results non-translation-invariant.
judgment.rationale: The issue identifies a clear numerical stability bug in the Birch clustering implementation. Following the human reviewer's correction, the label is updated to 'Numerical Stability' to accurately categorize the nature of the bug.

I propose we just port the runtime improvement without changing behavior; future work can look into adapting some of the other improvements.

- `SparseCoder` line 1412
- `DictionaryLearning` line 1750
- `MiniBatchDictionaryLearning` line 2334

3. `DictionaryLearning.fit_transform` returns the raw code `V` and never applies the
   split (the other two classes have no `fit_transform` override, so they are fine here)

`test_dict_learning_split` in `sklearn/decomposition/tests/test_dict_learning.py`, and it
only exercises `transform` and `inverse_transform` and no common test sets `split_sign=True`.

fix can be, make `_n_features_out` account for `split_sign` in all three,
allocate the split array with the input dtype, and have `fit_transform` apply the same
split `transform` does.

issue_title: OneHotEncoder unknown-category warning is incorrect for columns without an infrequent category
issue_body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Introduce yourself

I'm learning ML engineering and use scikit-learn for a delay-prediction model on
US flight data. This is the first issue I've opened. I encountered this while working out how to encode categorical columns that may contain previously unseen values during prediction.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Carrier and destination can't be enumerated ahead of time, so both go to one
encoder with `drop="first"`, `handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"` and
`min_frequency=4`. On my first CV fold, 41,901 rows, it fits to:

```
infrequent_categories_: [None, array(['HDN'], dtype=object)]
```

Destination gets an infrequent bucket. Carrier gets `None` because its rarest value has 148 rows in that fold and 744 across the training pool, so it is not below `min_frequency=4`. Transforming a row with an unknown carrier and an unknown destination produces this warning:

```
Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. These unknown
categories will be encoded as the infrequent category.
```

The warning claims that the unknown categories in both columns will go to the infrequent category, but this is not true for the carrier feature because no `infrequent_sklearn` column exists for it, and the transformed row is zero across the entire carrier block.

This matters because `drop="first"` drops the encoded feature for the first carrier category (`AA` in this fold), making all zeros its carrier encoding. An unknown airline and a real flight belonging to `AA` therefore produce an identical carrier encoding, so the model treats them the same with respect to the carrier feature.

I caught this by inspecting `infrequent_categories_`, transforming a row containing an unknown carrier and destination, and comparing the resulting vector with `get_feature_names_out()`. The carrier block was entirely zero, even though the warning said that the unknown carrier would be encoded as the infrequent category. The warning should have identified that the unknown carrier was encoded as all zeros, while the unknown destination was routed to its infrequent bucket.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import warnings

from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

# Column 0: "a" and "b" both appear twice, so it has no infrequent category.
# Column 1: "y" appears once, so it does have an infrequent category.
X = [["a", "x"], ["a", "x"], ["b", "x"], ["b", "y"]]

encoder = OneHotEncoder(
    drop="first",
    sparse_output=False,
    handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist",
    min_frequency=2,
).fit(X)

print("infrequent_categories_:", encoder.infrequent_categories_)
print("feature names:         ", encoder.get_feature_names_out())

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    X_trans = encoder.transform([["c", "z"]])

print("transform([['c', 'z']]):", X_trans)
print("warning:", caught[0].message)
```

Both columns receive an unknown category, but only column 1 has an infrequent
category that can absorb it.


### Expected Results

The warning should describe what actually happens to each column. Column 1 has
an infrequent category, so its unknown value is encoded there. Column 0 has
no infrequent category, so its unknown value is encoded as all zeros, which is the same encoding `drop="first"` assigns to the dropped category.

Something along the lines of:

```
Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. The unknown
categories in columns [1] will be encoded as the infrequent category. Those in
columns [0] will be encoded as all zeros, because these columns have no
infrequent category.
```

This is also what the `handle_unknown` docstring already documents:

> If the `'infrequent'` category does not exist, then `transform` and
> `inverse_transform` will handle an unknown category as with
> `handle_unknown='ignore'`.


### Actual Results

```
infrequent_categories_: [None, array(['y'], dtype=object)]
feature names:          ['x0_b' 'x1_infrequent_sklearn']
transform([['c', 'z']]): [[0. 1.]]
warning: Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. These unknown categories will be encoded as the infrequent category.
```

No exception is raised. The problem is that the warning talks about both columns and
makes a single claim about them, which is false for column 0: its
`infrequent_categories_` entry is `None`, no `x0_infrequent_sklearn` column
exists in `get_feature_names_out()`, and the transformed row is `0` across the
whole column-0 block.

Also reproduced on main (1.10.dev0) at a456b324bc, with identical output.

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I would be interested in opening a PR if this is triaged as a bug.

The warning message is selected once from `handle_unknown`, but the actual outcome is determined separately for each column in `_map_infrequent_categories` (`sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py`). I would update the warning to distinguish columns that have an infrequent category from those that fall back to all zeros, update the affected warning assertions, and add a regression test for the mixed case above.

judgment.summary: OneHotEncoder's warning message when handle_unknown='infrequent_if_exist' is misleading when some columns do not have an infrequent category, falsely claiming they will all be encoded as the infrequent category.
judgment.rationale: The issue describes a misleading warning message in OneHotEncoder (part of the preprocessing module) when handling unknown categories with 'infrequent_if_exist'. The actual transformation behavior is correct, but the warning is inaccurate for columns without infrequent categories. This is a low-priority bug/usability improvement.
